chapter_title: Alkyl Halides: Nucleophilic Substitution and Elimination Reactions

questions.chapter_title: Alkyl Halides: Nucleophilic Substitution and Elimination Reactions
questions.question: What is the mechanistic basis for the second-order rate law and complete stereochemical inversion in SN2 reactions?

options.label: A
options.text: The substrate ionizes first, followed by rapid nucleophilic capture from both faces.

options.label: B
options.text: The nucleophile adds to form a stable pentavalent intermediate that collapses.

options.label: C
options.text: The nucleophile attacks the substrate carbon simultaneously with leaving group departure in a single bimolecular elementary step: Rate = k[Substrate][Nu].

options.label: D
options.text: The reaction proceeds via homolytic radical substitution.

questions.correct_answer: The nucleophile attacks the substrate carbon simultaneously with leaving group departure in a single bimolecular elementary step: Rate = k[Substrate][Nu].
questions.explanation: SN2 is a concerted bimolecular displacement requiring simultaneous interaction of both reactants in the transition state.

questions.chapter_title: Alkyl Halides: Nucleophilic Substitution and Elimination Reactions
questions.question: What is the rate-determining step in the SN1 solvolysis of tert-butyl bromide in methanol?

options.label: A
options.text: Nucleophilic attack of methanol on the neutral alkyl bromide.

options.label: B
options.text: Deprotonation of the methyloxonium intermediate by solvent.

options.label: C
options.text: Unimolecular heterolytic cleavage of the C-Br bond to generate a planar tertiary carbocation intermediate and bromide ion: Rate = k[R-Br].

options.label: D
options.text: Formation of an alkene via E2 elimination.

questions.correct_answer: Unimolecular heterolytic cleavage of the C-Br bond to generate a planar tertiary carbocation intermediate and bromide ion: Rate = k[R-Br].
questions.explanation: The unimolecular loss of leaving group is the slow, rate-limiting step with the highest activation energy barrier.

questions.chapter_title: Alkyl Halides: Nucleophilic Substitution and Elimination Reactions
questions.topic: SN1 Stereochemical Outcome (Racemization with Inversion Excess)
questions.question: Why does SN1 solvolysis on a chiral secondary substrate often yield partial racemization with net inversion of configuration?

options.label: A
options.text: The nucleophile is completely blocked from the backside.

options.label: B
options.text: The reaction proceeds via a pure E2 mechanism.

options.label: C
options.text: The carbocation rotates into a chiral pyramid.

options.label: D
options.text: The departing leaving group partially shields the front face as an intimate ion pair, making backside attack by the nucleophile slightly more accessible.

questions.correct_answer: The departing leaving group partially shields the front face as an intimate ion pair, making backside attack by the nucleophile slightly more accessible.
questions.explanation: Intimate ion pair dynamics shield the retention face, leading to predominant but incomplete inversion alongside racemization.

questions.chapter_title: Alkyl Halides: Nucleophilic Substitution and Elimination Reactions
questions.question: Why does E2 elimination exhibit a strict requirement for anti-periplanar geometry (180° dihedral angle)?

options.label: A
options.text: Anti-periplanar alignment allows simultaneous constructive overlap of the breaking C-H σ bond and C-X σ* antibonding orbital into the developing π system.

options.label: B
options.text: The base is too small to reach the hydrogen in syn geometry.

options.label: C
options.text: The leaving group must collide directly with the base.

options.label: D
options.text: Syn-periplanar geometry creates a forbidden 10-electron intermediate.

questions.correct_answer: Anti-periplanar alignment allows simultaneous constructive overlap of the breaking C-H σ bond and C-X σ* antibonding orbital into the developing π system.
questions.explanation: Continuous π orbital overlap in the anti-periplanar transition state minimizes the activation barrier for alkene formation.

questions.chapter_title: Alkyl Halides: Nucleophilic Substitution and Elimination Reactions
questions.topic: E1 Mechanism Rate Law and Competition
questions.question: Why does the E1 reaction share the exact same rate law as the SN1 reaction on the same tertiary alkyl halide?

options.label: A
options.text: Both reactions proceed through a concerted pentacoordinate transition state.

options.label: B
options.text: Both reactions require two equivalents of strong base.

options.label: C
options.text: Both reactions share the identical rate-determining step: unimolecular ionization to form the tertiary carbocation intermediate.

options.label: D
options.text: Both reactions involve free radical intermediates.

questions.correct_answer: Both reactions share the identical rate-determining step: unimolecular ionization to form the tertiary carbocation intermediate.
questions.explanation: Since carbocation formation is the rate-determining step for both SN1 and E1, they share identical unimolecular kinetics: Rate = k[Substrate].

questions.chapter_title: Alkyl Halides: Nucleophilic Substitution and Elimination Reactions
questions.question: Why does potassium tert-butoxide (t-BuOK) favor the Hofmann (less substituted) alkene in E2 eliminations?

options.label: A
options.text: Hofmann alkenes are thermodynamically more stable than Zaitsev alkenes.

options.label: B
options.text: Steric clash between the bulky tert-butoxide base and substrate alkyl groups raises the activation energy for removing internal protons, funneling reaction to the accessible methyl protons.

options.label: C
options.text: tert-Butoxide reacts via an SN1 mechanism.

options.label: D
options.text: tert-Butoxide is a weaker base than ethoxide.

questions.correct_answer: Steric clash between the bulky tert-butoxide base and substrate alkyl groups raises the activation energy for removing internal protons, funneling reaction to the accessible methyl protons.
questions.explanation: Steric hindrance in the transition state prevents access to internal β-protons, making kinetic deprotonation of methyl protons much faster.

questions.chapter_title: Alkyl Halides: Nucleophilic Substitution and Elimination Reactions
questions.topic: Leaving Group Ability and pKa of Conjugate Acid
questions.question: Why is iodide (I⁻) a superior leaving group compared to fluoride (F⁻) in substitution mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.text: Iodine is more electronegative than fluorine.

options.label: B
options.text: Fluoride has a larger atomic radius than iodide.

options.label: C
options.text: Iodide is the conjugate base of a strong acid (HI, pKa ~ -10) with a large, polarizable 5p orbital that stably disperses negative charge in the transition state.

options.label: D
options.text: Fluoride forms weaker covalent bonds to carbon than iodide.

questions.correct_answer: Iodide is the conjugate base of a strong acid (HI, pKa ~ -10) with a large, polarizable 5p orbital that stably disperses negative charge in the transition state.
questions.explanation: Weak bases (conjugate bases of strong acids) with large polarizable electron clouds are excellent leaving groups.

questions.chapter_title: Alkyl Halides: Nucleophilic Substitution and Elimination Reactions
questions.question: Why do polar aprotic solvents like DMSO and DMF dramatically accelerate SN2 reaction rates?

options.label: A
options.text: They lower the boiling point of the reaction mixture.

options.label: B
options.text: They convert the alkyl halide into a free radical.

options.label: C
options.text: They form strong hydrogen bonds with nucleophilic anions.

options.label: D
options.text: They solvate cations effectively via oxygen dipoles but leave nucleophilic anions 'naked' and unencumbered by hydrogen bonds, raising their ground-state reactivity.

questions.correct_answer: They solvate cations effectively via oxygen dipoles but leave nucleophilic anions 'naked' and unencumbered by hydrogen bonds, raising their ground-state reactivity.
questions.explanation: Polar aprotic solvents do not hydrogen-bond with nucleophiles, significantly increasing nucleophile ground-state free energy and reaction rate.

questions.chapter_title: Alkyl Halides: Nucleophilic Substitution and Elimination Reactions
questions.topic: E2 Elimination Stereospecificity on Cyclohexyl Rings
questions.question: For an E2 elimination to occur on a substituted cyclohexane ring, what geometric condition must the leaving group satisfy?

options.label: A
options.text: The leaving group must be bonded to a bridgehead carbon.

options.label: B
options.text: The ring must be in a boat conformation.

options.label: C
options.text: The leaving group MUST occupy an axial position to achieve the required anti-periplanar geometry relative to an adjacent axial β-hydrogen.

options.label: D
options.text: The leaving group must be equatorial.

questions.correct_answer: The leaving group MUST occupy an axial position to achieve the required anti-periplanar geometry relative to an adjacent axial β-hydrogen.
questions.explanation: Only when both the β-hydrogen and the leaving group are diaxial (trans-diaxial) can an anti-periplanar 180° dihedral angle be attained.

questions.chapter_title: Alkyl Halides: Nucleophilic Substitution and Elimination Reactions
questions.question: What mechanistic consequence occurs when a substrate contains a neighboring thioether or alkoxide during substitution?

options.label: A
options.text: The neighboring heteroatom attacks intramolecularly to form a transient 3-membered cyclic onium ion, leading to retention of configuration and accelerated rate.

options.label: B
options.text: The substrate is oxidized to a carboxylic acid.

options.label: C
options.text: The reaction is completely stopped by steric hindrance.

options.label: D
options.text: The reaction changes into an E1 elimination.

questions.correct_answer: The neighboring heteroatom attacks intramolecularly to form a transient 3-membered cyclic onium ion, leading to retention of configuration and accelerated rate.
questions.explanation: Neighboring group participation proceeds via two consecutive SN2 inversions, resulting in net overall retention of stereochemistry.

questions.chapter_title: Alkyl Halides: Nucleophilic Substitution and Elimination Reactions
questions.question: What mechanistic consequence occurs when a substrate contains a neighboring thioether or alkoxide during substitution?

options.label: A
options.text: The reaction changes into an E1 elimination.

options.label: B
options.text: The reaction is completely stopped by steric hindrance.

options.label: C
options.text: The substrate is oxidized to a carboxylic acid.

options.label: D
options.text: The neighboring heteroatom attacks intramolecularly to form a transient 3-membered cyclic onium ion, leading to retention of configuration and accelerated rate.

questions.correct_answer: The neighboring heteroatom attacks intramolecularly to form a transient 3-membered cyclic onium ion, leading to retention of configuration and accelerated rate.

questions.chapter_title: Alkyl Halides: Nucleophilic Substitution and Elimination Reactions
questions.question: What is the mechanistic basis for the second-order rate law and complete stereochemical inversion in SN2 reactions?

options.label: A
options.text: The nucleophile adds to form a stable pentavalent intermediate that collapses.

options.label: B
options.text: The nucleophile attacks the substrate carbon simultaneously with leaving group departure in a single bimolecular elementary step: Rate = k[Substrate][Nu].

options.label: C
options.text: The substrate ionizes first, followed by rapid nucleophilic capture from both faces.

options.label: D
options.text: The reaction proceeds via homolytic radical substitution.

questions.explanation: SN2 is a concerted bimolecular displacement requiring simultaneous interaction of both reactants in the transition state.

questions.question: What is the rate-determining step in the SN1 solvolysis of tert-butyl bromide in methanol?

options.label: B

questions.topic: SN1 Stereochemical Outcome (Racemization with Inversion Excess)
questions.question: Why does SN1 solvolysis on a chiral secondary substrate often yield partial racemization with net inversion of configuration?

options.label: A
options.text: The departing leaving group partially shields the front face as an intimate ion pair, making backside attack by the nucleophile slightly more accessible.

options.label: B
options.text: The reaction proceeds via a pure E2 mechanism.

options.label: C
options.text: The nucleophile is completely blocked from the backside.

options.label: D
options.text: The carbocation rotates into a chiral pyramid.

questions.correct_answer: The departing leaving group partially shields the front face as an intimate ion pair, making backside attack by the nucleophile slightly more accessible.
questions.explanation: Intimate ion pair dynamics shield the retention face, leading to predominant but incomplete inversion alongside racemization.

questions.chapter_title: Alkyl Halides: Nucleophilic Substitution and Elimination Reactions
questions.question: Why does E2 elimination exhibit a strict requirement for anti-periplanar geometry (180° dihedral angle)?

options.label: A
options.text: Anti-periplanar alignment allows simultaneous constructive overlap of the breaking C-H σ bond and C-X σ* antibonding orbital into the developing π system.

options.label: B
options.text: The base is too small to reach the hydrogen in syn geometry.

options.label: C
options.text: Syn-periplanar geometry creates a forbidden 10-electron intermediate.

options.label: D
options.text: The leaving group must collide directly with the base.

questions.correct_answer: Anti-periplanar alignment allows simultaneous constructive overlap of the breaking C-H σ bond and C-X σ* antibonding orbital into the developing π system.
questions.explanation: Continuous π orbital overlap in the anti-periplanar transition state minimizes the activation barrier for alkene formation.

questions.chapter_title: Alkyl Halides: Nucleophilic Substitution and Elimination Reactions
questions.topic: E1 Mechanism Rate Law and Competition
questions.question: Why does the E1 reaction share the exact same rate law as the SN1 reaction on the same tertiary alkyl halide?

options.label: A
options.text: Both reactions involve free radical intermediates.

options.label: B
options.text: Both reactions proceed through a concerted pentacoordinate transition state.

options.label: C
options.text: Both reactions share the identical rate-determining step: unimolecular ionization to form the tertiary carbocation intermediate.

options.label: D
options.text: Both reactions require two equivalents of strong base.

questions.correct_answer: Both reactions share the identical rate-determining step: unimolecular ionization to form the tertiary carbocation intermediate.
questions.explanation: Since carbocation formation is the rate-determining step for both SN1 and E1, they share identical unimolecular kinetics: Rate = k[Substrate].

questions.chapter_title: Alkyl Halides: Nucleophilic Substitution and Elimination Reactions
questions.question: Why does potassium tert-butoxide (t-BuOK) favor the Hofmann (less substituted) alkene in E2 eliminations?

options.label: A
options.text: tert-Butoxide reacts via an SN1 mechanism.

options.label: B
options.text: Steric clash between the bulky tert-butoxide base and substrate alkyl groups raises the activation energy for removing internal protons, funneling reaction to the accessible methyl protons.

options.label: C
options.text: Hofmann alkenes are thermodynamically more stable than Zaitsev alkenes.

options.label: D
options.text: tert-Butoxide is a weaker base than ethoxide.

questions.correct_answer: Steric clash between the bulky tert-butoxide base and substrate alkyl groups raises the activation energy for removing internal protons, funneling reaction to the accessible methyl protons.
questions.explanation: Steric hindrance in the transition state prevents access to internal β-protons, making kinetic deprotonation of methyl protons much faster.

questions.topic: Leaving Group Ability and pKa of Conjugate Acid
questions.question: Why is iodide (I⁻) a superior leaving group compared to fluoride (F⁻) in substitution mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.text: Iodine is more electronegative than fluorine.

options.label: B
options.text: Fluoride has a larger atomic radius than iodide.

options.label: C
options.text: Iodide is the conjugate base of a strong acid (HI, pKa ~ -10) with a large, polarizable 5p orbital that stably disperses negative charge in the transition state.

options.label: D
options.text: Fluoride forms weaker covalent bonds to carbon than iodide.

questions.correct_answer: Iodide is the conjugate base of a strong acid (HI, pKa ~ -10) with a large, polarizable 5p orbital that stably disperses negative charge in the transition state.
questions.explanation: Weak bases (conjugate bases of strong acids) with large polarizable electron clouds are excellent leaving groups.

questions.question: Why do polar aprotic solvents like DMSO and DMF dramatically accelerate SN2 reaction rates?

options.label: A
options.text: They lower the boiling point of the reaction mixture.

options.label: B
options.text: They solvate cations effectively via oxygen dipoles but leave nucleophilic anions 'naked' and unencumbered by hydrogen bonds, raising their ground-state reactivity.

options.label: C
options.text: They convert the alkyl halide into a free radical.

options.label: D
options.text: They form strong hydrogen bonds with nucleophilic anions.

questions.correct_answer: They solvate cations effectively via oxygen dipoles but leave nucleophilic anions 'naked' and unencumbered by hydrogen bonds, raising their ground-state reactivity.
questions.explanation: Polar aprotic solvents do not hydrogen-bond with nucleophiles, significantly increasing nucleophile ground-state free energy and reaction rate.
